title: TIA -> aspirin; adverse effect = GI bleeding (COX-1 inhibition)
topic: Aspirin adverse effects / secondary stroke prevention
vignette: A 64-year-old woman comes to the hospital due to sudden-onset right arm weakness and difficulty speaking, which completely resolved within 20 minutes. The patient has had no shaking movements, headache, nausea, photophobia, or anxiety. She has a history of hypertension and hypercholesterolemia and takes amlodipine and rosuvastatin. Her blood pressure is 125/70 mm Hg and pulse is 78/min and regular. Neurologic examination is unremarkable. Fingerstick glucose is within normal limits. ECG shows normal sinus rhythm. Carotid Doppler reveals mild left common carotid artery stenosis. MRI of the brain and echocardiogram are unremarkable. If the patient is started on an additional medication that is indicated for her condition, which of the following adverse effects is most likely to occur?

clues.text: sudden-onset right arm weakness and difficulty speaking, which completely resolved within 20 minutes
clues.note: A focal neurologic deficit that resolves completely and quickly, with normal imaging, is a transient ischemic attack (TIA).

clues.text: mild left common carotid artery stenosis
clues.note: Carotid atherosclerosis is the likely embolic source; secondary prevention includes antiplatelet therapy (aspirin) plus risk-factor control.

clues.text: additional medication that is indicated for her condition
clues.note: For a noncardioembolic TIA, the indicated add-on is an antiplatelet agent - low-dose aspirin - whose hallmark adverse effect is the answer.

whatMatters: A transient focal deficit that fully resolves = TIA. Secondary prevention adds an antiplatelet - low-dose ASPIRIN. Aspirin irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX-1), impairing platelet function AND reducing prostaglandin-mediated gastric mucosal protection, so its most likely adverse effect is GASTROINTESTINAL BLEEDING. Answer B.
strategy: Identify TIA -> aspirin, then recall aspirin's signature toxicity via COX-1 inhibition: GI mucosal injury/bleeding (from decreased protective prostaglandins + impaired platelet aggregation). Reject effects of other drugs: CNS depression (benzodiazepines), hyperpnea/vertigo (salicylate TOXICITY at high doses, not routine low-dose), orthostatic hypotension (antihypertensives), sexual dysfunction (SSRIs/some antihypertensives), bladder cancer (pioglitazone).

eliminations.label: CNS depression - benzodiazepines/sedatives
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: sedation from GABA-potentiating drugs (benzodiazepines). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: aspirin does not cause CNS depression. ✅ Correct if: benzodiazepine or other sedative-hypnotic.

eliminations.label: Hyperpnea and vertigo - salicylate TOXICITY (your pick)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: high-dose salicylate poisoning causes tinnitus/vertigo and hyperpnea (respiratory alkalosis) with metabolic acidosis. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: these occur with salicylate OVERDOSE, not routine low-dose aspirin for stroke prevention; the expected common adverse effect is GI bleeding. ✅ Correct if: acute salicylate overdose (mixed acid-base disturbance).

eliminations.label: Orthostatic hypotension - antihypertensives
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: postural drops from vasodilators/volume depletion (alpha-blockers, nitrates, diuretics). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: aspirin doesn't cause orthostasis. ✅ Correct if: an antihypertensive with vasodilation.

eliminations.label: Sexual dysfunction - SSRIs / some antihypertensives
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: common with SSRIs and certain antihypertensives (thiazides, spironolactone, clonidine). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: not an aspirin effect. ✅ Correct if: SSRI or offending antihypertensive.

eliminations.label: Urinary bladder cancer - pioglitazone
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a long-term risk linked to the thiazolidinedione pioglitazone. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: unrelated to aspirin. ✅ Correct if: pioglitazone therapy.

reasoning: Transient focal deficit that fully resolves with normal imaging = TIA
Secondary prevention for noncardioembolic TIA adds an antiplatelet: low-dose aspirin
Aspirin irreversibly inhibits COX-1 -> impaired platelet aggregation + reduced gastric mucosal prostaglandins
mechanism: A transient ischemic attack (TIA) is a focal neurologic deficit from transient ischemia that resolves fully (here within 20 minutes) with normal imaging. For secondary prevention of noncardioembolic TIA/stroke, an antiplatelet agent - low-dose ASPIRIN - is indicated alongside blood-pressure and statin therapy. Aspirin irreversibly acetylates cyclooxygenase; at low doses it predominantly inhibits COX-1. Two COX-1-dependent effects raise upper GI bleeding risk: (1) inhibition of platelet thromboxane A2 synthesis impairs platelet aggregation, and (2) loss of prostaglandin-mediated gastric mucosal protection (reduced mucus/bicarbonate, increased acid, decreased mucosal blood flow) promotes mucosal injury. Even low-dose aspirin increases upper GI bleeding roughly 2- to 3-fold; a proton pump inhibitor can lower this risk. Thus the most likely adverse effect is gastrointestinal bleeding. The other options are toxicities of different agents (benzodiazepines, high-dose salicylate poisoning, antihypertensives, SSRIs, pioglitazone).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Pharm > aspirin: irreversible COX inhibition; low dose inhibits COX-1 -> ↓TXA2 (antiplatelet) + ↓gastric prostaglandins -> GI bleeding; salicylate toxicity (tinnitus, mixed acid-base) at high dose.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: TIA -> aspirin; its expected common adverse effect (low dose) is GI bleeding, not overdose-level tinnitus/hyperpnea.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on TIA, COX-1 vs COX-2, thromboxane A2, prostaglandin mucosal protection, or salicylate toxicity? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Hyperpnea/vertigo = salicylate OVERDOSE; CNS depression (benzodiazepines), orthostasis (antihypertensives), sexual dysfunction (SSRIs), bladder cancer (pioglitazone).

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: low-dose aspirin -> GI bleeding (COX-1: ↓TXA2 + ↓mucosal prostaglandins); PPI reduces risk.

keywords.front: Focal deficit fully resolving, normal imaging

firstAid.detail: Pharm: COX-1 inhibition -> GI mucosal injury/bleeding; antiplatelet effect.
Pharm > salicylate overdose (tinnitus/hyperpnea), pioglitazone (bladder cancer), SSRIs (sexual).
Neuro > antiplatelet + statin + BP control after TIA.

memoryHook: Aspirin muzzles COX-1 - platelets can't clot and the stomach loses its prostaglandin shield - so the classic price is a GI bleed.
